subject: Dedicated capacity sizing: KV cache sensitivity & quantization plan for Nucleus Bio

Subject: Re: Dedicated capacity sizing: quick context + numbers

Thanks Rishi — attaching the workload extract you asked for (NB-inference-workload.csv). A few clarifications up front: 

- Primary model: open-model family (g-model-xl-32k variant) with experiments at 32k and 64k context.
- Typical inference pattern: chat-style calls, median prompt ~4k tokens, 95th percentile ~24k tokens, occasional long-run batches hitting 40–64k tokens for full-genomics summaries.
- QPS: steady-state 6 rps, burst to 18 rps for 90s windows during nightly scoring jobs.
- P95 latency target: <= 350ms for user-facing chat flows; nightly batch can be higher.

Priority: we need a concrete committed configuration for Dedicated (reserved GPU pool) for budgeting and procurement. Appreciate the model/quant tradeoffs notes from Marissa yesterday — we want recommended GPU class, pod sizing, and a fallback policy if quantized variants introduce edge-case hallucinations.

Also looping in Procurement (procure@...) on schedule and supplier terms.

Thanks,
Ethan

Ethan — thanks for the data. Quick read and a few clarifying Qs before Priyom and Marissa put numbers on paper: 

- For the 64k runs, are most tokens in the prompt (prefix) or is the model generating the majority of the 64k? This changes KV cache persistence vs peak transient memory.
- Can you confirm percent of requests that include past convo history >16k tokens (so we can size prefix cache hit rate)?
- Any hard SLA windows where we cannot tolerate fallbacks to lower-precision variants (e.g., regulatory scoring where hallucinations are unacceptable)?

High-level plan we'll produce by EOD:
- Recommended reserved pod mix (GPU model + count) for steady-state + burst headroom.
- Memory profile per model variant (FP16 vs INT8 dynamic quant), expected KV.cache footprint per request, and expected impact on achievable batch sizes.
- Canary/fallback policy: 1) prefer quantized variant (INT8/4) for cost-sensitive flows, 2) automatic fallback to FP16 variant for flagged inputs or QA failures.

I attached the redwood-sizing-template.xlsx — fill the last two columns (expected % of requests per window and strictness of hallucination tolerance) and send back. Priyom and Marissa will use that to produce committed GPU counts for the deal.

Best,

From: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
To: Rishi Malhotra <rishi_malhotra@redwood.com>, Ethan Reynolds <ereynolds@nucleusbio.com>
Cc: Priyom Das <priyom_das@redwood.com>, Monica Patel <monica_patel@redwood.com>
Date: 2028-07-18T14:03:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Draft sizing notes — initial memory / pod sketch

Ethan / team — I pulled the CSV and sketched an initial memory model. High level findings below, followed by next-step asks.

Summary (TL;DR):
- Model variant: g-model-xl-32k (32k context FP16) needs ~42GB model + ~0.9MB/token KV for active attention states (KV cache). At 24k tokens active that's ~22GB KV. Total ephemeral GPU memory ~64–68GB before activation/buffer overheads.
- 64k context scenario (either using a 64k variant or windowed 32k with multiple prefix fetches) pushes KV cache to ~57GB; combined with model weights that requires a 120+ GB GPU effective address space -> recommends podting across 2 x A100-80GB-equivalent or 1 x H100-115GB with KV offload strategies.
- INT8 quantization reduces model weights memory 2.8x (approx), and KV per-token is unaffected by weight quantization; net GPU residency may drop below 80GB for many flows, enabling single 80GB pod for the 32k case.

Key tradeoffs and risks:
- Quantization gains are real for model weight residency, but do not reduce KV memory. Long-context workloads remain KV-bound.
- Offloading KV cache to host/NVMe with RDMA reduces GPU memory requirements but adds ~12–30ms tail latency depending on NVMe topology; might violate your P95 target for chat flows.
- Mixed-precision/partial-quantization (keep activations FP16, quantize weights) might be safest for regulated scoring where hallucination risk is high.

Concrete ask for you, Ethan:
- Confirm fraction of requests that must hit the P95 <= 350ms SLA (web chat vs post-processing). If >50% then offload options are likely unacceptable.
- Provide expected growth curve next 12 months (Q1/Q2/Q3 traffic multipliers).

I'll produce three committed pod proposals: conservative (H100 clusters, KV on-GPU, minimal quant), cost-optimized (INT8, single 80GB pods where possible), and hybrid (KV on host with latency SLAs for non-critical flows). Expect deliverable by tomorrow morning.

Marissa Cole
Solutions Engineering, Redwood Inference

Attachments referenced: internal sizing notes (not attached here)
From: Priyom Das <priyom_das@redwood.com>
To: Rishi Malhotra <rishi_malhotra@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>, Ethan Reynolds <ereynolds@nucleusbio.com>
Cc: Monica Patel <monica_patel@redwood.com>
Date: 2028-07-19T09:11:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Committed pod options + numbers (draft)

Team / Ethan — attached is a concise write-up of the three options Marissa mentioned plus the draft reserved counts for a 12-month commit at current QPS (steady 6 rps, burst 18 rps). Highlights: 

Option A — Conservative (SLA-first)- Pod: H100-115GB x1 per pod (weights + KV on-GPU)- Effective replicas: 10 pods steady to meet 6 rps with P95 headroom (we use continuous batching assumptions)- Burst headroom: +4 pods (autoscaling reserved)- Pros: meets 350ms P95; no NVMe latency- Cons: highest capex/commit

Option B — Cost-optimized (quant-first)- Pod: A100-80GB x1 with INT8-weight quantization (KV on-GPU for 32k flows)- Effective replicas: 6 pods steady (allows for higher batching)- Burst headroom: +6 pods for nightly scoring- Pros: ~40% lower monthly cost vs A- Cons: risk window for hallucination-sensitive scoring; 64k flows still problematic without KV offload

Option C — Hybrid (offload for background)- Pod: A100-80GB x1 + NVMe KV offload for nightly jobs- Effective replicas: 5 pods steady + NVMe-backed workers for long contexts- Latency trade: night batch ok; user-facing chat uses FP16 H100 lanes via a routing policy

Draft committed counts for Q1 (12-month): Option A = 14 reserved pods, Option B = 18 reserved pods, Option C = 12 reserved + NVMe pool (4 nodes). Numbers include 20% safety buffer.

Next steps: 
- Ethan: confirmation of P95 population and acceptance of quant risk by 7/19 COB.
- Procurement: we'll convert preferred option into a draft term sheet (I'll produce monthly committed costs).

Attachments: draft-MUTUAL-ACTION-PLAN.pdf (term sheet stub)

Thanks,
Priyom Das
Capacity Planning, Redwood Inference
From: Ethan Reynolds <ereynolds@nucleusbio.com>
To: Rishi Malhotra <rishi_malhotra@redwood.com>, Priyom Das <priyom_das@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
Cc: procurement <procure@nucleusbio.com>, Lia Chen <lia.chen@nucleusbio.com>
Date: 2028-07-19T17:42:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Finalizing committed option (we prefer hybrid)

Appreciate the thorough breakdown. After internal review with infra and procurement, Nucleus Bio is inclined toward Option C (Hybrid):

- Rationale: we need cost discipline for predictable spend but cannot risk P95 regressions for the web-facing use cases. Routing critical user-facing traffic to FP16 H100 lanes and offloading nightly scoring is acceptable.
- Ask: Can Redwood provide a concrete fallback routing policy (if NVMe latency > X ms, route to FP16 pool) and an automated roll-forward to INT8 for low-risk QA-labeled inputs?
- Contract ask: 12-month commit; target start 2028-09-01. Procurement will expect a line-item for NVMe pool support and a service credit clause if P95 > 350ms for user-facing route.

Ethan
Director, ML Engineering — Nucleus Bio
